name: Ianthe
domains: keeper of youths with Apollo and the Rivers

summary.text: Oceanid daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, named in Hesiod's catalogue among the holy company who, with lord Apollo and the Rivers, have youths in their keeping — also counted among the Oceanids who played with Persephone in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, as Pausanias reports.
summary.citation: Theogony 346–349; Fabulae, preface (Theogony); Description of Greece 4.30.4

story.text: Hesiod lists Ianthe among the daughters of Tethys and Ocean who share with Apollo and the Rivers the charge of youths all over the earth — in the same breath as Peitho, Admete, Electra, Doris, Clymene, Idyia, and Pasithoe. She receives no further episode in the poem beyond this custodial role.

Hyginus' genealogical preface names Ianthe among the Oceanides born of Ocean and Tethys — set beside Melite, Admete, Stilbo, Pasiphae, Polyxo, Eurynome, and Metis in his compressed register of the water-born daughters.

Pausanias, discussing when Fortune first entered poetry, cites the Homeric Hymn to Demeter: the daughters of Ocean who played with Kore in a lovely meadow included Leucippe, Phaeno, Electra, Ianthe, Melobosis, Tyche, and Ocyrhoe — placing this Ianthe among the divine playmates of Persephone, not among mortal Cretans.
story.citation: Description of Greece 4.30.4; Homeric Hymn to Demeter 5.420

story.text: The atlas keeps her apart from Ovid's mortal Ianthe of Crete, the golden-haired bride promised to Iphis in the Metamorphoses — a human girl of Phaestus, daughter of Telestes, who loved another maiden. That Ianthe belongs to a Milesian-Cretan tale of concealed sex; this Ianthe belongs wholly to Ocean's eldest daughters.
